title: Raven Steals the Light
text:
In the beginning, the Tlingit say, the world was dark. A rich and powerful chief who lived at the head of the Nass River kept the stars, the moon and the daylight shut up in boxes in his house, and guarded them jealously. Raven wanted the light, but he could not take it by force, so he found a way into the chief's family.

The chief had a daughter. Raven turned himself into a tiny hemlock needle and floated in her drinking water. She swallowed it without noticing, became pregnant, and in time gave birth to a baby boy. It was Raven.

The chief doted on his grandson. The child cried and cried, pointing at the boxes hanging on the walls. To quiet him, the grandfather gave him the bag of stars to play with. The child let them go up through the smoke hole, and they scattered across the sky. Then he cried for the moon, and after a long time the old man gave him that too, and it went up into the sky as well.

At last he cried for the box that held the daylight. When the chief finally gave it to him, Raven turned back into a bird, took the box, and flew out through the smoke hole. Later he opened it, and daylight spread over the whole world.
lesson: When a door is closed to force, find a way to become part of the household. Patience and access can win what open confrontation never would.
people: Raven, the chief who kept the light, his daughter
location: Southeast Alaska (USA) and the Nass River (British Columbia, Canada)
source: John R. Swanton, Tlingit Myths and Texts (1909)
caveat: Many versions exist among Tlingit, Haida, Tsimshian and other Northwest Coast peoples, and details vary between tellers.
